title: The Qur'an: where to start
hook: You already know two chapters by heart. Here's how to meet the rest.

screens.text: You already carry two chapters of the Qur'an by heart: al-Fatiha and al-Ikhlas. That's real. Today: what the rest of the book is, and an easy way to start reading it.

**What it is.** Muslims believe the **Qur'an** is Allah's own words, brought to the Prophet ﷺ by the angel Jibril over twenty-three years, in Arabic [Revealed Path ch. 10]. It has 114 chapters, each called a **surah**.

events.title: The first words
events.text: Jibril brought the first verses: recite in the name of your Lord, who taught by the pen [Q 96:1–5; Bukhari 3].

events.title: Piece by piece
events.text: It came in Arabic, a part at a time, until all 114 surahs were complete [Revealed Path ch. 10].

events.title: Kept safe
events.text: Memorized and passed down by millions, generation after generation. Muslims believe Allah promised to protect it [Q 15:9].

events.title: Your turn
events.text: Two of its surahs, al-Fatiha and al-Ikhlas, already live in your memory and your prayers.

options.feedback: Yes. 114 surahs, from long ones to a few short lines.
Not quite. Five is the number of daily prayers. The Qur'an has 114 surahs.

screens.title: Tap to flip: what new readers often think

cards.front: "I have to read it front to back, in order."
cards.back: You don't. It isn't arranged by date or as a story. Many people start with the short surahs near the end, or read a little from the beginning each day.
A translation shares the meaning, and it's how you'll understand it. The Qur'an itself is the Arabic, which is why prayer is in Arabic.
Muslims believe Allah promised to protect it [Q 15:9]. It has been memorized and passed down by millions, generation after generation [Revealed Path ch. 10].

cards.front: "It's too hard for someone like me."
cards.back: The Qur'an says it was made easy to remember [Q 54:17], and whoever struggles reading it gets a double reward [Muslim 798].

screens.text: **Where to start.** Pick a clear English translation with short notes; ask {{mentor.name}} which one your masjid recommends. Read five or ten verses a day, slowly.
bubbles: Stop when something touches you. Listening to recitation while you read the English helps too.
Little and often beats a big push. The Prophet ﷺ praised those who learn the Qur'an and teach it [Bukhari 5027].

screens.title: Read your first five verses (2 minutes)
screens.intro: Have two minutes now? Try it. If not, come back to it today.

steps.text: Open the Qur'an in the app's reader at chapter 96 (al-'Alaq)
Listen to verses 1–5 once in Arabic
Notice: the very first word revealed was about reading and learning
Say "alhamdulillah" (all praise is for Allah): you've just read the first verses ever revealed

screens.done_text: That's how it started for the Prophet ﷺ too: five verses.

variant.default: **Respect for the book.** Most scholars say to have wudu before touching a printed Arabic Qur'an (a **mushaf**). Your masjid will tell you its view on apps and translations, and on reciting while you need a ghusl. Listening is fine any time.
variant.hanafi: **Respect for the book.** Have wudu before touching a printed Arabic Qur'an (a **mushaf**). An app (without touching the words) and reciting from memory are fine without wudu, unless you need a ghusl. Listening is fine any time [First Instructions on Worship Part I].

screens.prompt: Ana wants to read some Qur'an on her phone during her lunch break, but she doesn't have wudu. What's right?

options.text: She can read it on the app; wudu is for touching a printed mushaf
options.feedback: Right. Reading on an app is fine without wudu (some say don't touch the words). Wudu is for holding the printed Arabic copy.

options.text: She can't read any Qur'an without wudu
options.feedback: Not quite. Reading on an app or from memory doesn't need wudu. Touching a printed mushaf does.

options.text: She should wait until she can read Arabic
options.feedback: Not quite. Read the translation now. Understanding it is the point, and Arabic can come later.

prayerPhrase.arabic: سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ وَتَبَارَكَ اسْمُكَ وَتَعَالَى جَدُّكَ وَلاَ إِلَهَ غَيْرُكَ
prayerPhrase.translit: Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika, wa tabarakasmuka, wa ta'ala jadduka, wa la ilaha ghairuk
prayerPhrase.meaning: You are perfect, O Allah, and I praise You. Your name is blessed, Your greatness is high, and no god exists but You
prayerPhrase.when: Quietly, right after the opening Allahu akbar, before al-Fatiha. First rak'ah only. [Abu Dawud 776; Tirmidhi 243]

Not quite. Make wudu before touching a printed mushaf.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- The Qur'an: Allah's words, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ through Jibril over about 23 years, in Arabic; preserved by memorization and writing [Revealed Path ch. 10; Q 15:9]. First revelation: [Q 96:1–5; Bukhari 3]. 114 surahs, not in chronological order.
- Made easy to remember [Q 54:17]; the struggling reader is doubly rewarded [Muslim 798]; the best learn and teach it [Bukhari 5027].
- Translations convey meaning; the recitation in prayer is Arabic only (Q13: never offer a translation to recite in prayer).
- Hanafi: wudu is required to touch a mushaf; someone needing ghusl may not recite Qur'an or touch a mushaf [First Instructions on Worship Part I]. Many contemporary Hanafi scholars allow reading on a device without wudu but advise not touching the verses on screen.
- Opening du'a (*Subhanaka Allahumma…*) is sunnah in the Hanafi school, said quietly after the opening takbir in the first rak'ah; a follower says it too, before the imam begins reciting aloud [Abu Dawud 776; Tirmidhi 243; First Instructions on Worship ch. 7].

**Likely questions**
- *"Which translation?"* Suggest asking the mentor for the masjid's recommendation; Saheeh International (the one this app quotes) is a common clear choice. Don't rank translators.
- *"Which surahs first?"* The short surahs in the last section (e.g., chapters 112–114, 103, 108), and al-Fatiha's meaning.
- *"I read a verse about war / women / punishment and it bothered me."* Take it seriously; give context briefly (verses have settings and are explained by scholars); offer to go through it slowly or route to the imam. Don't dismiss the discomfort or argue.
- *"Can I touch the Qur'an on my period?"* Not a printed mushaf (Hanafi); she can listen and read the translation. Reciting: see Day 17's scholar flag.
- *"Do I need to learn Arabic?"* Not to be a good Muslim; the prayer phrases are enough now. Learning the Arabic letters is optional, Day 82.

**Escalate:** interpretation of specific contested verses beyond a brief mainstream summary; questions about the Qur'an's preservation that turn into serious doubts (take them seriously, offer a scholar).

**Don't**
- Don't interpret verses with a personal ruling; stay with mainstream summaries.
- Don't quote translations other than Saheeh International from the Citation Bank.
- Don't make Arabic sound like a requirement to belong.
madhabNote:
- **Opening du'a:** the Hanafi school uses *Subhanaka Allahumma…*; Shafi'is often use a longer du'a beginning *Wajjahtu wajhiya…*; Malikis don't say an opening du'a in obligatory prayers. Any authentic opening is valid where it's said.
- **Touching a mushaf:** all four schools require wudu to touch a printed Arabic Qur'an, with small differences over translations, devices and children learning.
